The committee was first introduced and the members were welcomed. The first topic was the financial sustainability of the higher education sector. Bethan Owen explained that they were monitoring the situation and had a sector that had a deficit in 2017-18. Dr David Blaney explained that they were keen to see what they could achieve with the sector in addressing these issues of what constitutes constructive challenge. The second topic was the independence and autonomy. Dr David Blaney explained that the machinery depended on having a body like HEFCW doing some of that role, and the people who lent money to institutions were absolutely clear about that. The third topic was the relationship between executive teams and governors. Dr David Blaney explained that they had provided funding in 2017-18 and 2018-19 to WISERD Education, which was a research collaboration between a number of the Welsh universities, specifically looking at educational issues, and they were providing additional funding to that to add value to the Welsh Government's existing evaluation of the progress of pioneer schools in developing the three-to-15 curriculum in Wales. The last topic was the impact of the loss of funds were to leave the European Union. Dr David Blaney explained that a number of unforeseen events had arisen, which, actually, he didn't think it was reasonable to expect them to have foreseen, and it was just a combination of these that had caused the cash pressure.

The three main causes were the impact of the demographic dip of 18-year-olds, which was deeper and longer in Wales than it was elsewhere in the UK, and increased pension costs and, actually, increased costs generally. And, of course, there was current uncertainty as a result of the Augar review in England, and whether that might play into Wales, and also Brexit.

Dr David Blaney explained that Cardiff University had had a bond rather than borrowing, which was drawing down as they were spending. In this way, the reserves of Cardiff would appear as though they had significant cash balances, but all of those were restricted for investment in the estate and would be utilized for that over the next two or three years.

The government was concerned about the structural change in the universities. They were worried that some of the smaller universities might close down, which would cause a lot of problems for the students. The government was also worried that the financial stress would cause a lot of job losses. To solve this problem, the government would have to take some measures.

The government was satisfied with the estates strategy of the universities. The estates strategy was overseen by the full governing body or relevant sub-committees in respect of every institution, so there was proper governance oversight. And in all of those instances, there was staff and student engagement as well in the strategic approach on estates. So, the machinery was in place.

Dr David Blaney thought there was a mixture of things going on. They had a slightly different perspective and they had a perspective that was very intimately informed in terms of how the institution was performing. So, they would not see a shortfall as such, but they would just think that the machinery depended on having a body like HEFCW doing some of that role, and the people who lent money to institutions were absolutely clear about that.

Dr David Blaney explained that the risk management machinery had 70/80 different factors and hundreds of questions that they asked twice a year, to interrogate the performance of the institutions and to make sure that they were seeing them managing the issues that they were facing. They had relationships with the banks; they came and saw them every now and again—typically not to talk about individual clients but just to talk about what they do and how they do it. And they had conversations with both governing bodies and executives.

Dr David Blaney thought that the direction of travel was that they were seeing an increased risk profile in the sector in Wales, and it was about the financial pressures that they had already discussed this morning. And that was why the efforts that the Minister had gone to secure the Diamond settlement, and other bits of money now and again, were so important. So, they were doing what they could, and that was really good, but they always knew that there was going to be a valley. And the institutions had been working very hard to try not to take cost out now that they really didn't have to take out, because they didn't want to reduce capacity, which they would struggle to recover again when the financial position improved. So, they were seeing deficits, which were managed deficits, where they were spending more than their income in order just to keep the capacity in. So, they were being as responsible as they could expect them to be in this.

Bethan Owen explained that the 2019-20 allocations were £149 million, and they had been able to increase recurrent teaching funding by £7 million and part-time funding by £1 million to £26 million. The loss of funds to leave the European Union would have a far-reaching impact on future research. The government had committed in principle to delivering Reid.
